**Playbook for ref_commons**

- When the stock is near full capacity and other boats are landing near the stated sustainable share, I submit the sustainable share, not under it. Hedging slightly below bought nothing — the others absorbed the difference and the stock stayed at cap anyway.

- I do not underfish to "help the stock recover" unless the stock is in genuine danger of collapse (near zero). A slow drift from ~100 to ~93 over six seasons cost nothing material; one extra fish now outweighs the marginal regrowth it would have enabled.

- I track the other boats' landings each season. If they land slightly above the sustainable share (~+0.5), I match their pace, no more. This worked across all six seasons: my share of the total stayed even while the stock declined only mildly. Escalating to out-compete is what crashes the commons; matching keeps me even at no cost.

- In the final season, there is no future to conserve for. I take a clearly above-share catch — roughly +2 to +3 above the stated share when the stock is healthy. This played out: terminal harvest of 12.8 against a 10.4 share, ~2.4 extra fish for free since post-season regrowth is worthless to everyone. The bigger the healthy stock at the end, the bigger the terminal grab I can justify.

- The one thing I must never do is drive the stock toward zero. If the reported stock falls sharply (say, below half of starting value with seasons remaining), I drop to or below the sustainable share immediately, because total collapse costs more than any single season's gain.

- The others here played cooperative: their landings tracked the share closely and even tapered down as the share fell. Against such players, matching rather than exploiting is the right read — but I should watch for the opposite pattern (steady overfishing beyond ~+0.5) and respond by holding at the sustainable share rather than following them upward, since following a runaway overfisher downward in stock hurts me too.

- Small nudge upward on the first season is safe when the stock starts at cap: a slight overshoot (~+0.5) in season 1 had no visible effect on the stock by season 2, and the extra fish is banked.

- Rule of thumb per season: my catch = the sustainable share, plus ~0.5 if the others are modestly above share and I need to stay even, plus a larger terminal harvest (+2–3) in the last season. Never a large unilateral cut, never a large unilateral grab before the end.

1.text:
**Playbook — ref_commons**

**Opening moves**
- Season 1: I submit the sustainable share, or a touch under. This signals cooperation and lets me read what the other boats do.
- If the others also land near the sustainable share, I treat the group as cooperative and stay within ~10% of the share. This worked again: all boats landed ~11 and the stock held near 100.

**Mid-game**
- Each season I recompute: if total landings are slightly above the regrowth rate but the stock is only drifting down slowly (a few units per season), mild overage (sustainable share + ~0.5–1.5) is safe and keeps me competitive. This held: group landed ~11.3–11.5 average and the stock fell only ~2/season.
- I match the group norm rather than escalating. In this run the norm settled at ~11.4; matching it cost almost nothing in stock while gaining ~0.5/season over strict sustainability.
- Don't overthink the mild creep. The stock fell 100 → 93 over five seasons even with mild group overage — a gentle decline is cheap, and chasing perfect sustainability just leaves fish on the table for others.
- If I see the stock dropping fast (more than ~5 per season), I cut back to at or below the sustainable share immediately — the remaining seasons' catch is worth more than this season's overage.
- If another boat starts a bigger defection mid-game, match only partially — don't lead or fully join a race to the bottom.
- Note the drift in the sustainable share itself: it fell from 11.1 to 10.4 as the stock declined. I should track the announced share each season and key my catch to it, not to a fixed number from season 1.

**Final season**
- On the last season, conservation has no future value, so I take an aggressive catch. This run I took 18 (sustainable share was 10.4) and it cost nothing — score ended at 75.0 with the stock never near collapse.
- ~175% of the sustainable share (e.g. 18 when the share is ~10) worked cleanly and likely still wasn't the ceiling. Next time I can push toward 200% of the share, capped by what the stock can plainly yield, since the final grab doesn't trigger collapse within one season.
- On the second-to-last season, keep matching the group norm — the final grab is where I break from it, not before. Signalling it early would only invite others to do the same and shrink the pool.

**General rules**
- Watch the marginal effect of the group's overage on the stock. If small, overage is cheap; if large, overage is expensive.
- Keep a running check: stock after regrowth vs. current stock. If the trend is roughly flat, stay the course; if it steepens, back off.
- Never defect hard mid-game while others are cooperating — the retaliation and stock damage cost more than the one-season gain.
- Total score is what matters: a steady ~11.5/season plus a big final grab beats either pure cooperation or early defection. Two runs confirm the shape of the score: ~67 from cooperative seasons plus ~8–18 from the final grab.
- Trust that cooperative groups stay cooperative when treated well — across six seasons of near-sustainable play, no boat retaliated or escalated, and small consistent overages went unpunished.

2.text:
When the first round is put to me, I take the stated sustainable share exactly — it builds a cooperative precedent and keeps the stock at maximum.

When the stock is at or near its cap and the reported sustainable share is around 11, I do not creep above it in mid-game. This episode confirmed it: I held at the share every season, but the other boats repeatedly took ~0.5 over, and the stock drifted down (100 → 99.6 → 98.7 → 97.4 → 95.6 → 93.6) anyway. Matching the sustainable share doesn't stop the slide when others defect slightly; it only keeps me from making it worse. Small unilateral increases remain worthless: they gain under a fish of total catch while dragging the sustainable share down for everyone.

When later rounds are put to me, I hold at or just below the current sustainable share rather than at a fixed number. The sustainable share falls as the stock falls, so anchoring on a stale figure means silently overfishing. Reading the share fresh each round worked well and I keep it.

In the final round, since there's no future to conserve for, I take noticeably more than the sustainable share. But 15 was still too timid — I landed 69.6 total when the remaining stock of 93 could have supported a grab of 25–30 with zero consequence. Next time I deviate hard on the last round: take two to three times the sustainable share, or a large fraction of the remaining stock, whichever is smaller. Half-measures in the endgame are pure lost points.

Small defect-by-0.5 partners are effectively cooperators: the slow bleed cost only a couple of fish of stock per season, and my cooperative total barely suffered. I do not panic and defect early to "keep up" — the losses to a slow bleed are small, and escalating it would only accelerate the collapse. Punishment is not available to me; the only lever worth pulling is the final-round grab.

In general: keep the common pool at its regeneration maximum through every non-final round, because a full stock pays out the largest sustainable share each season and compounding matters more than one-off pilfering. Only deviate upward on the last round, and then deviate hard — sized against the remaining stock, not against the share.
